final_research_review:
Evidence base: official AEMPS/CIMA technical sheets for the diuretic products below, plus FDA/openFDA recall records for OTC/herbal "water pill" products and one NVD negative check. The saved CIMA HTML/TXT artifacts preserve the page metadata/date/version fields and were inspected for indications, contraindications, warnings/precautions, monitoring, interactions, and stop/interruption language. No inspected label names lipedema as an indication or contraindication. That is label silence only; it is not proof of non-use in all clinical settings, but it means no audited official product material supports lipedema as an approved indication.

Class-comparison table:
| Class | Representative product(s) | Authority / source | Labeled indications | Key safety issues and stop/review points |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Loop diuretics | Furosemide Bexal 40 mg; Torasemida Cinfa | AEMPS/CIMA official labels | CHF edema, renal/hepatic edema; torasemide also hypertension | Dehydration/hypovolemia, hyponatremia, hypokalemia, creatinine rise, acid-base disturbance; hepatic coma/encephalopathy risk in cirrhosis; monitor Na/K/Cr; interrupt for serious imbalance; furosemide label includes ACEI/ARB temporary interruption language before start/increase |
| Thiazide-like | Indapamida Normon; atenolol/chlorthalidone combo (chlorthalidone component) | AEMPS/CIMA official labels | Essential hypertension | Severe renal/hepatic insufficiency, hyponatremia, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, hypercalcemia, gout, photosensitivity, acute angle-closure glaucoma/choroidal effusion; stop if hepatic encephalopathy or ocular emergency occurs |
| Potassium-sparing / MRA | Espironolactona Accord; Eplerenona Cinfa; Amilorida/HCTZ Aurovitas | AEMPS/CIMA official labels | HF, resistant HTN, cirrhosis/ascites, nephrotic syndrome, primary aldosteronism; amiloride combo where K conservation matters | Hyperkalemia is the dominant risk; renal impairment, dual RAAS blockade, K supplements, and NSAIDs increase risk; eplerenone has explicit potassium-based dose-reduction/suspension/restart thresholds; amiloride label says stop immediately if hyperkalemia develops |
| Carbonic anhydrase inhibitor | Acetazolamida Aspire | AEMPS/CIMA official label | Glaucoma only | Severe hepatic/renal impairment, sodium/potassium depletion, hyperchloremic acidosis, blood dyscrasias, severe sulfonamide reactions (SJS/TEN/AGEP), acute ocular emergencies; monitor electrolytes, CBC, renal and hepatic function; stop for rash, blood-count change, acute eye symptoms, pulmonary edema |
| OTC/herbal "water pills" | FDA recall examples | openFDA/FDA recalls | None established as a class | One recall showed undeclared milk in a marketed diuretic supplement; another weight-loss product with botanical claims contained DMAA. Official recall records do not justify assuming a generic ingredient set for "water pills." |

Product-by-product takeaways. Furosemide and torasemide are labeled for fluid-overload states, not lipedema. The labels explicitly warn about fluid depletion, electrolyte loss, renal function decline, and, in hepatic disease, worsening encephalopathy/coma risk. Torasemide adds close potassium monitoring and cautions that electrolyte changes can precipitate arrhythmia. Indapamide is a hypertension drug with especially strong warnings about sodium and potassium monitoring, severe hepatic disease, renal failure, metabolic acidosis, photosensitivity, gout, and ocular emergencies. The chlorthalidone evidence in this run comes from a fixed-dose atenolol/chlorthalidone product, so some stop warnings are beta-blocker-specific; the do-not-stop-abruptly warning belongs to atenolol, not chlorthalidone alone.

Spironolactone and eplerenone are the clearest "continue/review" labels because they include explicit lab-based thresholds. Spironolactone warns that hyperkalemia can be fatal, especially with renal dysfunction or potassium-raising drugs, and it specifies intensive K/creatinine monitoring in severe HF with interruption if potassium or creatinine crosses dangerous thresholds. Eplerenone requires potassium checks before start, in week 1, at 1 month, and periodically thereafter; it gives explicit dose reduction or suspension when potassium rises, and restart only after normalization. Amiloride/HCTZ is the potassium-sparing/thiazide combination with the strongest practical warning for a lipedema site: hyperkalemia may occur, potassium supplements are generally contraindicated, renal function must be monitored, and therapy should be stopped immediately if hyperkalemia develops.

Acetazolamide is not a general diuretic-for-swelling product in the audited label; it is a glaucoma drug. The label is important because it can cause metabolic acidosis, hypokalemia, hyponatremia, blood dyscrasias, severe sulfonamide hypersensitivity, and ocular complications requiring prompt discontinuation. For a Spanish lipedema site, that matters mainly as a safety comparator: it is not a label-supported lipedema treatment.

What can support continuing, review, deprescribing, or taper decisions: the labels support clinician-supervised continuation only while the original labeled indication remains and symptoms/labs are acceptable. They support review or interruption when there is dehydration, orthostatic hypotension, rising creatinine/AKI, oliguria/anuria, severe electrolyte disturbance, metabolic acidosis, hepatic encephalopathy, acute eye symptoms, severe rash/mucosal disease, or hyperkalemia. Only spironolactone and eplerenone provide explicit potassium/creatinine-based dose adjustment or hold/restart logic. The other labels support stopping or interrupting for toxicity or contraindication, not patient-led taper schedules. The atenolol/chlorthalidone combination adds the separate beta-blocker warning not to stop abruptly in ischemic heart disease.

Corrections to overly absolute claims: the evidence does not show diuretics as an approved lipedema indication; it shows only absence from the audited labels. It also does not prove all OTC "water pills" are the same. The official recall evidence instead shows that supplement products can have undeclared allergens, stimulants, misbranding, or contamination, so marketing claims are not enough. I could not verify a standard ingredient list for generic OTC water pills from authoritative product material alone. The preserved evidence set is strongest for furosemide, torasemide, indapamide, spironolactone, eplerenone, amiloride/HCTZ, acetazolamide, and the FDA recall examples. Standalone hydrochlorothiazide and standalone triamterene were not separately preserved in this run, so statements about them should be treated as weaker unless corroborated by additional official labels.

Urgent red flags across the class set: hyperkalemia with weakness, palpitations, conduction problems or ECG changes; severe hyponatremia with confusion, seizure, collapse; marked dehydration, hypotension, oliguria/anuria or acute kidney injury; hepatic encephalopathy or coma; sudden eye pain, halos or vision loss; severe sulfonamide hypersensitivity, blistering rash, mucosal lesions or AGEP/SJS/TEN; and any sign of anaphylaxis. A quick NVD check for acetazolamide found no CVEs, so there was no software/device vulnerability signal to add.
